articles.title_orig: Traders start to move US copper to China as Trump tariff fears ease
articles.title_zh: Traders start to move US copper to China as Trump tariff fears ease
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”

articles.title_orig: America, China, and the Costs of the Bipolar AI Race
articles.title_zh: America, China, and the Costs of the Bipolar AI Race
articles.content_orig:
We are in the age of artificial intelligence. Many are comparing the technology to electricity and describing it as the industrial revolution of this century. The United States has long dominated the field, but China’s meteoric rise has made it the strongest challenger to American dominance . The AI race is increasingly bipolar, and much of the power to shape this critical technology is concentrated in these two countries.
With the American and Chinese dominance of this emerging technology comes a widening geographic divide that begins with who builds AI technologies and where. As the great power rivalry between Washington and Beijing intensifies, most other countries increasingly rely on AI technologies but have little say in how those systems are built, tested, and governed.
These technologies are entering schools, hospitals, and government offices around the world, but decisions about what makes these systems safe and how much control people retain are made largely elsewhere. So are the decisions about whose values frontier models reflect and which languages they support.
The bipolar concentration of AI power has heightened the sense of vulnerability outside the U.S. and China and given a new urgency to the efforts of various countries to build sovereign models of their own.
For now, the future of AI in the rest of the world depends on the U.S. and China. Take the computing infrastructure needed to build the most advanced AI models, also known as frontier models. Between 2022 and June 2026, the U.S. received roughly 72% of the world’s new AI computing capacity, according to estimates by Epoch AI, a research organization. China received 10%. That left a mere 18% for all other countries combined.
This concentration extends beyond AI chips. The International Energy Agency estimates that the U.S. and China accounted for about 70% of the electricity consumed by data centers worldwide in 2024, while data centers in the rest of the world consumed a meager 30%. Research and development infrastructure for AI is similarly concentrated in the U.S. and China. A Carnegie Endowment study of more than 10,000 researchers who published at NeurIPS, a leading AI conference, in 2025 found that three-quarters were affiliated with employers in the U.S. or China.
Even if we set aside the energy and physical infrastructure needed to build frontier models, significant gaps in training data and language coverage remain. Consider the question of languages and representation. Most of the world’s roughly 7,000 languages remain poorly supported by AI , even though about 3.4 billion people speak them. The data used to train frontier models and the benchmarks used to evaluate them largely leave these languages out.
A recent snapshot of Common Crawl, a web archive widely used to train language models, revealed that roughly 43% of the pages were in English . A mere 0.2% were in Hindi, a language spoken by more than half a billion people. In a 2025 study , my colleagues and I found that training data for Quechua, a language spoken today by about 8 million people, primarily across South America, included texts from the era of Spanish colonization.
Developers of most frontier models rely heavily on publicly available data on the internet, which contains biases and harmful content my colleague Claire Wardle described as the “armpit of the internet.” In fact, my research has shown that frontier models can act as a powerful force for cultural and linguistic homogenization while reproducing gender , disability , caste, and religious biases .
I have been studying and evaluating how AI affects the way people in different cultures express themselves in writing. I have consistently found that when users in India write with AI assistants, their writing styles shift to mimic those of Americans, and their language loses some of its cultural nuance. The suggestions of AI assistants also influence and change how these users describe their cultural norms and express their views on a range of social issues.
Even the cost of using AI can depend on the language you speak. AI companies often charge by the token, a unit of text. The same message can require more tokens in Hindi and Odia than in English. Newer systems have narrowed this gap but have not eliminated it. Thus, developers building AI-driven apps in Hindi or Odia can face a language tax, paying more to process the same content than they would in better-supported languages such as English, Mandarin, or Spanish.
The rest of the world has little control over American and Chinese frontier models, and even access to them can depend on decisions made in Washington or Beijing. In June, citing national security concerns, the U.S. government ordered Anthropic to block foreign nationals—including those on its own staff—from accessing Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models. Anthropic responded by taking both models offline for all users. The restrictions were lifted later that month, but the episode exposed how quickly a single government’s decision can cut off access to technologies used around the world.
The incident invigorated the efforts of several middle powers to build sovereign models of their own. A handful of middle powers have charged ahead and developed their own models: Sarvam in India, Cohere in Canada, Mistral in France, and Jais in the United Arab Emirates. Their developers have sought to make these models more responsive to local needs, contexts, and languages.
To gain more control over the technology and protect their national interests, the governments of India and Canada are moving quickly to invest in domestic AI firms, including through equity stakes. In the UAE, Jais was developed by a partnership involving Inception, a subsidiary of G42, which is chaired by Sheikh Tahnoun bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the country’s national security adviser and a member of Abu Dhabi’s ruling family. Here, the term “sovereign” can take on a literal meaning.
Yet it remains unclear how powerful these sovereign models are or how well they reflect local cultures and contexts. Many sovereign models are built by adapting open-weight models developed in the U.S. or China and can inherit biases from those models. As our study shows, some regional models can write fluently in local languages while misreading the social norms and contexts of their speakers. Knowing how to speak a language is not the same as understanding the social norms of its speakers or how their schools, hospitals, and government offices work.
Training data contribute to these failures. But developers also train models to favor some responses over others—a process called “alignment.” One common approach asks people to compare AI-generated responses and choose which they find more helpful or less harmful. Those judgments are then used to train models, shaping how they respond to millions of users.
Yet the people and languages represented in this feedback do not adequately reflect the world’s diversity. For instance, in a 2022 Anthropic study , feedback was collected in English, and roughly 20 paid online workers accounted for about 80% of the data. Even Meta’s more recent Community Alignment project , designed to help models respond to different cultural preferences, draws on participants from only two countries in the Global South and includes English and Hindi, but none of the hundreds of other languages spoken in India.
It is also difficult to reliably and systematically measure how safe these models are in local contexts. Existing safety tests cover too few languages and cultural contexts in the Global South and often assess isolated responses rather than conversations that unfold over multiple exchanges.
Can these sovereign AI models compete with the frontier models? This challenge is especially daunting since frontier models have ushered in a new era of scientific discovery and uncovered cybersecurity vulnerabilities in digital and physical environments, including critical national infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.title_zh: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.content_orig:
Wes Streeting told Volodymyr Zelensky he was in Kyiv to show that Europe was united in its support for Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He also rejected the claim the Russian president made in China that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimean Bridge
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders met in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys to discuss Ukraine.
That meeting came hours after Putin held trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.
Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title_orig: Denmark expels Russian diplomat over alleged plot to kill Ukrainian rapper
articles.title_zh: Denmark expels Russian diplomat over alleged plot to kill Ukrainian rapper
articles.content_orig:
COPENHAGEN, Denmark — Authorities thwarted the attempted killing of a Ukrainian American citizen on Danish soil in a plot allegedly orchestrated by Russian intelligence services, the Danish prime minister’s office said Friday.
The Russian defense attaché has been expelled from Denmark in response, Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. Two alleged members of the outlawed Danish gang “Loyal to Familia” have been arrested in connection with the attempted killing, police said.
Danish broadcaster DR, citing a court hearing, reported the men are suspected of having been recruited to assassinate ​a Ukrainian rapper ahead of a planned performance.
Police thwarted the alleged plot when they arrested ​the two men shortly before the rapper ​Kyivstoner’s September 25 concert, which was later ⁠cancelled.
It was unclear how police identified the two men, who ​were stopped in ​a vehicle ⁠carrying several weapons, or how the investigation expanded to include two other men ​who are not accused of participating ​in ⁠the alleged assassination plot targeting Kyivstoner.
However, all four men have been held in custody since September, according to ⁠the ​broadcaster.
It was also unclear how ​the Russian intelligence services allegedly recruited the two Danish suspects.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said: “It is a clear illustration of the grave security situation Denmark and Europe find ourselves in. We are facing a Russia under pressure which is acting more aggressively and is more willing to take risks.”
The Danes’ announcement came as tensions between Europe and Russia heightened again Friday. Two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine.
European Commission ​President Ursula von der Leyen said on Saturday the E.U. ⁠stands in full solidarity with Denmark.
“This was an ​attack ⁠on E.U. ‌soil. And it is unacceptable. We stand in full ‌solidarity with Denmark. ‌And with all Member States targeted by Russian ⁠hybrid attacks,” she said in an X post.
European Council President António Costa said: “We will not be intimidated. Russia’s tactics and threats will not weaken the European Union’s resolve to continue supporting Ukraine.”
The Russian embassy in Copenhagen said on Friday the accusations were not backed ‌with proof.

articles.title_orig: Nations at UN talks on AI killer robots agree to more talks but no firm commitment to rein them in
articles.title_zh: Nations at UN talks on AI killer robots agree to more talks but no firm commitment to rein them in
articles.content_orig:
An armed robot developed by Turkish defense companies is demonstrated at a facility in Duzce, Turkey, on April 29. Omer Urer/Anadolu via Getty Images hide caption
Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as U.N.-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years.
Scores of countries ended the week-long U.N. conference on weapons by agreeing to "elaborate" a possible accord on such lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. But they didn't commit to binding rules sought by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, many countries, and activists.
The outcome underscored the difficulty of achieving concrete results in diplomacy amid global conflicts and major military powers jockeying for dominance.
Izumi Nakamitsu, the U.N. high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a "significant achievement" but acknowledged a "glass half full or half empty" scenario, citing Guterres' hopes for a legally binding deal this year.
Activists accused military powers like Russia and the United States of blocking stronger language.
Stop Killer Robots lamented a "watered-down mandate," and Beatrice Fihn, founder of international law advocacy group Lex International, said the decision amounts to "pushing the can down the road for two more years."
They noted most countries supported work toward a new treaty, and Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute, said: "States have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue, for the 14th year, while these weapons enable atrocities."
Before the meeting, seven countries proposed launching negotiations on a rulebook that could prevent or limit the ability of machines to kill without human control or accountability. That effort fell short.
"Technology is moving faster than diplomacy," said Ambassador Frederico Meyer of Brazil, which joined Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama in proposing such negotiations. "Diplomats are very slow."
After years of talks on the issue, advocacy groups bemoaned obstructionism largely by Russia, which, like other top AI weapons-developing countries such as the United States, wants a freer hand to develop such high-tech weapons.
Guterres, who leaves office at the end of the year, set a 2026 deadline for launching negotiations toward an agreement on autonomous weapons systems.
Pope Leo XIV and many advocacy and humanitarian groups have framed the issue as an existential debate, urging quick action to rein in AI weapons before they become too commonplace to regulate easily.
Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones, but widespread rollout hasn't happened.
Talks this week centered on the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, ratified by 128 countries, where decisions are made by consensus. That means any single country can thwart an agreement, and that any deal was likely to be based on a low common denominator.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.title_orig: The Danger of Jensen Huang’s Handshake Deals at Nvidia
articles.title_zh: The Danger of Jensen Huang’s Handshake Deals at Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
The still-unraveling scandal of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's extramarital affairs and the tech giant's potential role in its advanced semiconductor chips ending up in China present a legal minefield for Huang and Nvidia.
Federal and state prosecutors and Nvidia employees may target Huang and the company in court, where some shareholders have already taken action.
That's on top of a rapidly growing pile of probes by Republicans who control Congress now and Democrats who will have majorities in both the House and Senate come January.
"It's not going to get any better for Jensen Huang; it's going to get far worse," said Salvatore Graziano, a New York securities litigation attorney at Bernstein, Litowitz, Berger & Grossmann. His firm is looking at shareholder lawsuit opportunities against Nvidia and Huang.
[Huang] "faces the Department of Justice, the Securities and Exchange Commission and private litigation," Graziano said. "The criminal exposure is very serious. The SEC could bar him from being an officer. And the potential liability [from shareholder] lawsuits can be very large."
Huang's and Nvidia's legal exposure stems from three issues that led up to his shock resignation Nov. 12.
There's his alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, who worked for Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company under investigation for diverting advanced Nvidia semiconductor chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules. That, in turn, has raised questions about whether Huang and Nvidia were aware of any diversions.
There are Huang's two other alleged affairs with Nvidia employees.
And there is the sharp drop in the company's stock price in the wake of the scandal. Nvidia's share price has fallen 19% since Nov. 8, when Huang sent a company-wide apology acknowledging extramarital affairs.
Huang last week retained the law firm Paul, Weiss and its attorneys Melinda Haag and Walter Brown to represent him. Haag is a former U.S. attorney in San Francisco, and Brown is also a former federal prosecutor.
Huang's spokesman at Trident, a crisis communications firm, declined to comment when asked if Haag and Brown are representing him in any potential criminal case and other questions about his legal exposure.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. Last week, Nvidia retained the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an independent investigation into Huang allegedly being targeted by a spy, as U.S. intelligence reportedly has concluded.
The civil liability Huang and Nvidia could face is underscored by a hearing Graziano, the securities attorney, attended Tuesday in U.S. District Court in San Francisco. A judge at the hearing approved a $175 million settlement from Seagate Technology Holdings to resolve a shareholder lawsuit alleging it concealed sales of hard-disk drives to Huawei in China in violation of export bans.
The Seagate settlement came three years after the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security — which is investigating Megaspeed's business with Nvidia — imposed a $300 million penalty on Seagate for its sales to Huawei.
Graziano said his law firm is "actively looking at securities law liability for Nvidia, Jensen Huang and other senior executives in the company given all the recent developments regarding their [potential] knowledge and facilitation of illegal chip sales to Chinese entities."
There is already a pending class-action shareholder lawsuit in San Francisco federal court against Nvidia and Huang by the Rosen Law Firm , for allegedly misleading and false statements related to Megaspeed and Alice Huang.
"Several hundreds of investors have contacted us and expressed an interest to join the case — investors of all walks of life, from mom and pops to investors with very large losses," Rosen attorney Phil Kim told CNBC in an email.
Katie Sweeten, a former federal prosecutor in the DOJ's National Security Division, said the question of "who knew what and when, and what was [Huang's] role" is potentially the biggest risk for Nvidia and him.
"Now DOJ can leverage their criminal authorities," Sweeten, a partner at Scale LLP, told CNBC's Kelly Evans on "The Exchange."
"They can bring grand jury subpoenas, search warrants for emails, bank accounts, personal devices, computers, things like that," Sweeten said.
While it is "not illegal to, you know, sleep with a spy ... it is illegal to pass certain types of information to a counterintelligence officer," she said .
Sweeten also pointed to potential export control violations, which "could be very serious."
She noted the DOJ can indict a company as well as its officials if there is evidence of criminality. Export control violations carry a maximum possible criminal sentence of 20 years in prison and "really large fines," she said.
"You can't send the company to prison, but they can face fines, civil penalties, debarment — where you can't export items down the line," she said.
One example of that came in July 2025, when the DOJ obtained a guilty plea and an agreement to pay more than $140 million from Cadence Design Systems for violating the Export Control Reform Act by unlawfully exporting semiconductor design tools to China's National University of Defense Technology, a school led by China's Central Military Commission.
Another potential legal risk for Huang comes from his planned appearances before Congress.
Huang is scheduled to give a closed-door interview Dec. 1 to three House committees. Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., wants Huang's testimony before that panel to be public, and told CNBC Tuesday he hopes to have that happen "before Christmas."
Sweeten said Huang "has to be very careful" about what he says there because of the risk of being criminally charged with lying to Congress, and of saying something "that absolutely can become part of a criminal or civil investigation."
"I expect Huang to take the Fifth on most questions" from Congress, Jonathan Kanter, a former assistant attorney general in the DOJ's Antitrust Division, told CNBC, meaning Huang will likely use his constitutional right against giving testimony that could be used against him in a criminal case.
"With a Justice Department criminal investigation into Megaspeed already underway and more investigations possible, anything he tells Congress could be used against him," Kanter said. "His lawyers are likely to advise him against taking that risk."
Ben Heineman Jr., a former senior vice president and general counsel of General Electric , and a senior fellow at Harvard University, told CNBC that Nvidia's board will be scrutinized over its actions before it pushed Huang to resign.
Heineman cited the board's apparent lack of succession planning and what looks like weak oversight of Huang, including relating to personal conduct such as the two alleged affairs with Nvidia employees and with an executive of an Nvidia customer.
"When there is a sort of reasonable suspicion, they need to investigate it, and they don't appear to have done that," Heineman said.
Nvidia and Huang could face investigation from state attorneys general, including in California, where the company is headquartered.
On Tuesday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta told Bloomberg Television that the situation at Nvidia with Huang is "something that we're interested in." Bonta's office later told CNBC, "We are monitoring the situation."
Huang's alleged affairs with Nvidia employees also open the possibility of workplace litigation.
Ari Wilkenfeld, a Washington-area employment lawyer, said a consensual relationship between a chief executive and a subordinate "is not in and of itself illegal."
"The liability never comes from the existence of the relationship alone. It comes from whether it was genuinely welcome, what job benefits flowed from it, and what it did to everyone else in the building," Wilkenfeld said. articles.title_orig: Grand Theft Auto VI Hits 60 FPS and Above on Xbox Series X Through a Quick Resume Glitch, but Gameplay Runs at Double Speed
articles.title_zh: Grand Theft Auto VI Hits 60 FPS and Above on Xbox Series X Through a Quick Resume Glitch, but Gameplay Runs at Double Speed
articles.content_orig:
In true Rockstar Games tradition, Grand Theft Auto VI launched with a 30 FPS target on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S due to technical reasons, as even the PlayStation 5 Pro's CPU cannot handle the game's complex simulation at 60 FPS . However, besides using some PC tools to bring the framerate of streamed console gameplay up to 60 FPS or higher, there's a way to enjoy the latest entry in the series at an unlocked framerate on Xbox Series X via a glitch, though with some catches.
The Grand Theft Auto VI FPS unlock glitch was discovered by Reddit user Meowwie64 , who detailed the entire process on the GTA6unmoderated subreddit :
"I somehow unlocked my framerate on GTA VI via a weird glitch within the Xbox's Quick Resume Feature that allows GTA VI to run at an unlocked framerate ."
1. An Xbox Series X (Maybe does work on Series S too can't test it myself, though)
3. Grand Theft Auto VI (on Game Version 01.002.001; this glitch may still work on later versions not sure)
1. Put your Xbox display settings to 60Hz
3. Wait until you see the 6 Stars in the Intro
4. Change your display settings back to 120Hz
5. Cold Boot another game on your console via the Xbox Guide (The Xbox button) and without quitting GTA VI
7. Now enjoy GTA VI at an unlocked framerate"
As mentioned above, there are some catches. As the game speed is tied to animation, something that was rather common in past generations, Grand Theft Auto VI essentially speeds up when the framerate goes beyond the 30 FPS lock. However, looking at the footage shared by the user, cutscenes do work well even at 60+ FPS.
Given that Grand Theft Auto VI can run at 60 FPS or higher on Xbox Series X , one can only wonder why Rockstar Games still targets 30 FPS on all systems. Although we can only speculate at this point, it's likely related to overall performance stability. As the framerate often dips below 30 FPS even on the PlayStation 5 Pro , it's likely that a 60 FPS target or an unlocked framerate would have produced jarring performance swings, resulting in anything but an enjoyable experience.
About the author : Francesco De Meo has been covering video games and technology since 2012, starting his career at small outlets like Gamersyndrome and GeekSnack. 

After joining the Wccftech gaming section in 2015, he quickly expanded his video gaming coverage with in-depth reporting, interviews with iconic industry figures such as Grasshopper Manufacture founder and No More Heroes creator Goichi "Suda51" Suda, Resident Evil series creator Shinji Mikami, Team NINJA's president and Nioh series director Fumihiko Yasuda, and Silent Hill creator Keiichiro Toyama, reviews and on-the-ground coverage of major industry events such as Gamescom and E3.

When he's not reporting or reviewing, Francesco can be found playing the genres he loves most, spending time with his six cats, reading, writing music, playing guitar and drumming for his progressive rock band.

articles.title_orig: Iraqi Forces Enter Stronghold of Powerful Iran-Backed Militia
articles.title_zh: Iraqi Forces Enter Stronghold of Powerful Iran-Backed Militia
articles.content_orig:
JURF AL-SAKHAR, Iraq — Iraqi security forces deployed in Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah armed group , on Friday under a deal that seeks to limit the reach of Iran’s most powerful Shi’ite militia ally in the country without provoking a confrontation.
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi this week ordered security forces to move against the heavily armed Kataib Hezbollah , which officials accused of running an oil smuggling network siphoning state-owned oil worth hundreds of millions of dollars in Jurf al-Sakhar.
The hardline Kataib Hezbollah (Battalions of the Party of God), branded a terrorist group by the United States, has rejected the smuggling accusations, which have led to arrests that prompted fears of an armed response . The group is among those that have claimed attacks on US forces in Gulf states since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
A convoy of vehicles flying Iraqi flags headed into Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday and soldiers took up positions in the center after senior security officials told a press conference that government forces would protect the town.
Members of the Kataib Hezbollah group stood near their group’s flags.
“From Jurf al-Sakhar, we begin asserting state authority across all of Iraq, confronting corruption and weapons beyond state control,” Zaidi told government troops who entered the town, speaking from a military operations center in Baghdad.
“Our decision is firm: No weapons outside state authority, no weapons but Iraq‘s, no decisions but Iraq‘s, and no flag shall fly higher than the Iraqi flag.”
Under the arrangement, brokered by Shi’ite politicians, Kataib members were expected to withdraw to other parts of Iraq , a major oil producer and ally of both the US and Iran.
“God willing, things will be safe and secure with the presence of the security forces,” said resident Mohamed Ali.
The deal will include the opening of a security headquarters in Jurf al-Sakhar on Saturday to oversee the handover. Iraq‘s energy police have begun securing an oil pipeline in Jurf al-Sakhar, the state news agency reported.
“Today is a historic moment in which the Iraqi Armed Forces prove that they are the nation’s shield, safety valve, and the guardian ensuring security stability for the Iraqi people,” Sabah al-Numan, spokesperson for the commander-in-chief of the Iraqi armed forces, told the press conference.
Reflecting the sensitivity of the situation, Iraqi Shi’ite political figures said Esmail Qaani , commander of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards’ Quds Force, arrived in Baghdad on Monday to help defuse tensions with Kataib Hezbollah.
So far, nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed following an investigation focused on Jurf al-Sakhar in Babil province, about 50 km (30 miles) south of Baghdad.
Any direct confrontation with Iran’s heavily armed militia allies in Iraq could be risky.
After one of Zaidi’s predecessors ordered a similar crackdown on those armed groups five years ago, the prime minister’s Baghdad home was hit in a drone strike that authorities described at the time as an assassination attempt.
US President Donald Trump has pressured Zaidi to disarm the militias that have struck US troops and facilities in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in solidarity with Tehran since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in February.
Kataib Hezbollah and other militias, all of whom report directly to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, have refused to hand over their weapons to the state.
Founded in the aftermath of the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq, Kataib is among the most influential members of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq , the umbrella group of hardline Shi’ite armed organisations supported by Iran.
Kataib Hezbollah quickly developed a reputation for deadly attacks against military and diplomatic targets during the US-led counterinsurgency war and sectarian conflict of the 2000s, using snipers, rockets, mortars and roadside bombs.
Since the 2003 US-led invasion toppled Iran’s arch-enemy, longtime Sunni leader Saddam Hussein, Tehran has steadily expanded its influence in Iraq through close ties with heavily armed Shi’ite militias and political parties.
Iraqi security officials say the militias’ arsenals include assault rifles, machineguns, anti-tank guided missiles , mortars, precision-guided rockets, armed drones and some short-range ballistic and cruise missile capabilities.
Kataib has its own political party, called Huquq, or Rights, with five lawmakers. An Iraqi official report said the group also generates cash through businesses such as construction, housing, trade, tourism and currency exchange, though Kataib denies this and says it is dedicated to security .
Pro-Iranian militias, including Kataib, enjoy a semi-official status in Iraq, which critics say encourages them to act with impunity. A shadowy group with no announced leadership structure, Kataib Hezbollah has thousands of hardened fighters.
It forms several battalions in Iraq‘s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), a grouping of armed factions set up in 2014 to fight Islamic State and subsequently recognized as an official security force.
Fighters receive state salaries and Kataib Hezbollah members, including some designated as terrorists by the US, hold senior positions in the PMF. While it is technically under the command of Iraq‘s prime minister as part of the PMF, the group often operates outside the chain of command.

articles.title_orig: Heat pumps can heat homes for €2.20 a day in winter, study finds
articles.title_zh: Heat pumps can heat homes for €2.20 a day in winter, study finds
articles.content_orig:
Europeans brace for what could be a particularly cold winter this year, after an unusually early sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) flipped the polar vortex.
The polar vortex is a ring of westerly winds that keeps freezing polar air locked over the North Pole about 30km above the Earth’s surface.
Sometimes, large atmospheric waves can disrupt this circulation, causing the winds to weaken significantly or even reverse direction. This can cause temperatures in the stratosphere to rise rapidly.
As the cold air from high up in the stratosphere disperses, it can affect the shape of the jet stream as the cold air sinks from the stratosphere into the troposphere, which extends from the ground up to an average altitude of about eight to 15 kilometres.
According to market intelligence provider Montel , forecasters warn that this "heightens the odds of colder temperatures”, more storms, wind and heating demand on the continent over the next month.
However, analysts say this would need to be a “repeated event” to have a sustained effect throughout the winter, as single SSW events are “short-term in nature”.
A severe cold spell could put gas supplies under even more pressure, following warnings from the EU that it may have to curb its gas consumption by seven per cent this winter as stocks hit record lows for this time of year.
Dwindling gas reserves, primarily driven by the war on Iran and subsequent blockade of the Strait of Hormuz – one of the world’s biggest fossil fuel shipping routes – are also set to worsen ahead of a full ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports from January 2027.
The unusually early SSW “might make people a bit nervous”, says Klaas Dozeman, energy forecaster at Brainchild Commodity Intelligence, adding that “most meteorologists remain puzzled on what the effects will be over the coming weeks”.
Green technology is cushioning Europe from the ongoing fossil fuel crisis, providing more households with energy security and lower bills.
Solar power , for example, has already saved the EU €44.6 billion in avoided gas imports since the beginning of the US-led war on Iran, which started on 28 February.
But as the days get shorter and darker, it is heat pumps that will offer relief from spiralling energy prices.
Heat pumps, which work by capturing energy from air, water or the ground and turning it into heat or cold air, typically deliver three to four kWh of heat for every one kilowatt-hour (kWh) of electricity they consume.
Each residential heat pump installed displaces around 1,100 m3 of gas and two tonnes of CO2 per year on average, if the small amount of electricity it uses to run is from renewable sources.
Europe’s heat pumps provide as much heat as the LNG carried by more than 200 tankers, according to an analysis from the European Heat Pump Association published in June*.
This is double the amount that arrived in the EU in 2025 from the Middle East and around seven per cent of the EU’s total annual imported LNG – avoiding €9.7 billion in import costs last year.
“Every heat pump installed is another bolt in the door of European energy security,” says Paul Kenny, director general of EHPA.
“LNG is the most expensive energy source and comes from unreliable suppliers, and heat pumps can drastically reduce our need for it.”
Despite myths suggesting that heat pumps do not work in cold countries, which Euronews Earth has debunked here , new research has found that when used effectively, air source heat pumps could help heat homes on a typical winter day for as little as £1.84 (approximately €2.20) a day.
The study, from British property developers Barratt Redrow, found that heat pumps can be more efficient than traditional gas boilers because they keep a more constant temperature rather than relying on spikes of heat.
"Heat pumps will run during the cold but consume a lot more power,” Jean-Paul Harreman, Director at Montel, tells Euronews Earth.
“The efficiency is better from a heat pump than from a gas boiler, but if power prices go really high, high costs might still be seen during the worst of the cold. However, that is usually only part of the winter, so a price spike should not be confused with an annual total cost.”
Heat pump sales rose 13 per cent last year, hitting 2.9 million in 21 European countries. This brings the total stock to 29.3 million.
When asked whether heat pumps could help the EU’s dwindling gas supply, Harreman said: “A little yes. We see electrification of heating happening in many countries, but the overall impact on demand is not that large.
“Industrial demand destruction plays a bigger role.”
Industrial demand destruction is a sustained or permanent drop in industrial consumption of energy caused by prolonged high prices or supply constraints.
*EHPA’s data is based on 21 EU member states. You can read the full analysis here .

articles.title_orig: Moscow Rejects Kaja Kallas as Europe Pushes for Role in Ukraine Peace Talks
articles.title_zh: Moscow Rejects Kaja Kallas as Europe Pushes for Role in Ukraine Peace Talks
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Russia warned that EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas’s participation in Ukraine peace negotiations would derail the process, accusing her of hostility toward Moscow. The warning came as European leaders sought a role in US-mediated talks and Vladimir Putin proposed preliminary discussions with European envoys. Kallas insists Russia must agree to a ceasefire before negotiations on Europe’s wider security architecture.
Russia warned Friday, Nov. 20, that the participation of EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas in negotiations over Ukraine would lead to the collapse of peace efforts, as Moscow stepped up its attempts to influence who represents Europe in talks over the war.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova declared that Kallas was unacceptable to Moscow, accusing the former Estonian prime minister of hostility toward Russia and opposition to its security demands.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“If anyone in Brussels is interested in such a negotiator with Russia, it merely demonstrates to us clearly what results they hope to achieve in dialogue with us – the derailment of any peace initiatives,” Zakharova said at a briefing in Moscow.
She added that Kallas would accomplish such a task “with flying colors.”
The warning came as European governments sought a formal role in US-mediated negotiations involving Ukraine and Russia, insisting that decisions affecting Europe’s security cannot be made without European participation.
Kallas has repeatedly maintained that Moscow has no right to determine who represents the EU in diplomatic negotiations.
She has also called for an immediate ceasefire and Russian concessions before discussions move toward a broader European security settlement.
Zakharova accused Kallas of adopting an “openly Russophobic stance” and rejecting Russia’s security concerns.
She claimed that the EU’s top diplomat was determined to undermine any settlement that acknowledged Moscow’s interests.
The Russian spokeswoman said Moscow remained willing to engage with European representatives capable of making a constructive contribution to negotiations, but argued that Kallas did not meet that standard.
Kallas, who served as Estonia’s prime minister before becoming the EU’s foreign policy chief in December 2024, has been among Europe’s most outspoken advocates of tougher sanctions against Russia and sustained military assistance to Ukraine.
She has consistently rejected Russian demands for restrictions on Ukraine’s sovereignty, military capabilities and future security partnerships.
The latest Russian statement represents a direct challenge to the EU’s authority to choose its own diplomatic representatives.
Earlier this month, Kallas acknowledged that Moscow opposed her participation but emphasized that she represented all 27 EU member states rather than speaking in a personal capacity.
Kallas has argued that Moscow is attempting to shift negotiations away from ending its invasion toward rewriting Europe’s broader security arrangements.
Speaking ahead of an EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting in Brussels on Monday, Nov. 16, she warned that Russia was repeating sweeping demands first presented before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“The Russian demands are maximum demands and really absurd,” she said, accusing Moscow of using negotiations to extract concessions without offering meaningful compromises.
Kallas insisted that an immediate ceasefire must precede talks about Europe’s future security architecture.
“What we need to see is [a] ceasefire,” she said. “A ceasefire to actually start the talks about anything else.”
She also criticized the expectation that Europe should make concessions to Moscow while Russian forces continue attacking Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
“They are the aggressor, and there is one victim. We need to seek concessions from their side,” Kallas said.
She identified sanctions and frozen Russian assets as important sources of European leverage, warning against granting Moscow concessions without receiving anything in return.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

articles.title_orig: Zelda's Ocarina Remake Is One Of Metacritic's Highest-Rated Games In 2026, According To User Scores
articles.title_zh: Zelda's Ocarina Remake Is One Of Metacritic's Highest-Rated Games In 2026, According To User Scores
articles.content_orig:
It's been a huge year for the games industry with all sorts of heavy-hitters releasing over the past few months, and as we look towards the end of 2026, we're now checking in on Metacritic's highest-rated games of the year based on the user score .
While Grand Theft Auto 6 may have officially surpassed Ocarina's Remake as the highest-rated game of 2026 on the review aggregate website (and also matched the original N64 hit as the highest-rated critic Metascore of all time ), it seems the classic outing on Switch 2 has won players' hearts worldwide.
According to the latest update from the site, Ocarina's Remake is currently sitting in the top highest-rated games (above 90), based on user score (it's on 9.2/10 at the time of writing). It's in good company with other games like Resident Evil Requiem and Splatoon Raiders .
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
Obviously, there are all sorts of different factors in play here when it comes to user scores (and the system in place isn't necessarily perfect). For example, Ocarina's Remake has over 25,000 user reviews , whereas other titles may have around 100 reviews. Keep in mind, user scores are also subject to change over time.
And if you're wondering how GTA 6 has been received by players, it's currently sitting on a user score of 5.5/10 after more than 30,000 user reviews . Even with supposed review bombings , it might take some time before it wins over some players. Despite top marks from critics, this new entry in the GTA universe appears to have divided the fanbase in its opening week.
As attention shifts towards the end-of-year game awards, both Ocarina and GTA 6 have already been nominated for multiple industry awards.

articles.title_orig: Israeli settlers' move into a Palestinian neighborhood brings deadly violence to Jericho's doorstep
articles.title_zh: Israeli settlers' move into a Palestinian neighborhood brings deadly violence to Jericho's doorstep
articles.content_orig:
Bullet hit 72-year-old Fadha Wadha in head outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, in the West Bank, say residents
A 72-year-old Palestinian woman has been shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli settlers in a village near Jericho where settlers have recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.
Fadha Wadha was standing outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta in the occupied West Bank when she was struck in the head by a bullet as Israeli settlers fired towards Palestinian houses, according to testimonies from residents. Several other Palestinians, including her son, were wounded by gunfire.
Abu Younis, a cousin of Wadha’s husband, told the Guardian that the violence had begun when a group of settlers attacked a young boy they accused of entering a courtyard seized from its Palestinian residents.
Dozens of Israeli settlers, some of them armed, moved into eight buildings in al-Duyuk al-Tahta two weeks ago with the backing of the settler organisation Nachala and a regional council representing illegal settlements in the central West Bank.
“A vehicle carrying settlers chased him,” Younis said. “There were about 15 settlers in several vehicles. They began firing indiscriminately, killing the woman.”
Witnesses said Palestinian residents began to throw stones to defend themselves, as more settlers arrived at the scene, shooting at civilians and injuring six men.
Wadha’s son, Arafat Fidhat, was wounded after he rushed to the scene after learning that his mother had been shot. His wife, Naama Fidhat, told Reuters he was in shock when he accidentally collided with a parked car belonging to one of the settlers.
Witnesses said the vehicle was empty at the time, but that settlers responded by opening fire, wounding Arafat in the torso.
Naama Fidhat said her husband was being taken to a hospital in Ramallah when Israeli soldiers stopped the ambulance and arrested him. She said Israeli soldiers also arrested their son, Wadha’s grandson, early the following morning.
“What did we do? We didn’t do anything,” she said. “This is our house, they were the ones who came with weapons … we were unarmed, we were sleeping.”
The Israeli military said a group of Palestinians in ​a car “accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it”. It said the Palestinians exited the vehicle and attacked the Israelis, who opened fire at the Palestinians. “There are Israeli and Palestinian ​casualties in the incident,” the military said.
The arrival of the Israeli settlers in al-Duyuk al-Tahta had raised fears among Palestinian residents who have faced repeated attacks in the area.
The Binyamin regional council, which covers 47 illegal settlements, claimed the properties in the village had been bought from Palestinians, but Jericho’s governor, Hussein Hamayel, disputed the claim, saying the land belonged to the state and could not legally be sold.
Human rights activists said settlers had assaulted and robbed two Israeli activists and shot a Palestinian man in the leg during the takeover earlier this month.
“Since the settlers moved into the area on 4 November our lives have been turned upside down,” Younis told the Guardian. “We used to live peacefully and safely on our farms, but since the settlers arrived, our lives have become a living hell. I own 53 dunams [5.3 hectares] of farmland with greenhouses, but we are no longer allowed to access them. We have suffered devastating financial losses, and now people are being killed as well.”
There has been a sharp ​rise in attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the West Bank, territory Israel captured in the 1967 six-day war. UN bodies and most ​countries deem the settlements illegal, which Israel disputes.
On Tuesday, Suleiman Abu Srour, a photographer for the Palestinian news agency Wafa, was beaten by Israeli soldiers while covering events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta . Wafa said he suffered fractures and bruises, was detained for six hours and had his phone confiscated before being released.
Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion, ethnic cleansing and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
articles.title_zh: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
articles.content_orig:
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent Alpöge said on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut , that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named after the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.
OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.
The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths and physics .
A group of maths scholars said AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.
The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths , external and physics , external .
A group of maths scholars said , external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released , external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

articles.title_orig: Trump formally ends minting of the penny after nearly 250 years of production
articles.title_zh: Trump formally ends minting of the penny after nearly 250 years of production
articles.content_orig:
Washington is officially done with spending a pretty penny on penny production .
President Donald Trump on Friday signed the bipartisan Common Cents Act , which formally directs the federal government to stop minting the penny.
Both the House and the Senate passed the measure by voice vote, meaning no notable opposition.
“It costs nearly FOUR cents to make just one penny,” the bill’s author, Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., said Sept. 29 on X a day after Senate passage . “This legislation will save $85 million per year by permanently ending penny production — it’s common sense!”
The U.S. Mint last year put the immediate annual savings of discontinuing penny production at $56 million .
The government stopped making pennies in November 2025 , nine months after Trump called for the Treasury Department to stop production , writing at the time that the process was “so wasteful!” However, the U.S. Mint said it would still produce collector versions to be produced in “limited quantities.”
The penny can still be used as legal tender “for all debts, public charges, taxes, and dues,” according to the new law. The Treasury Department said last year that the Federal Reserve will continue to recirculate the approximately 114 billion pennies that are in existence “for as long as possible.”
The new measure also provides a procedure for stores and businesses that accept cash payments to round their prices to the nearest amount divisible by 5 cents.
And, as the nickel replaces the penny at the bottom of the U.S. Mint’s currency list, that coin can now be manufactured with an inner layer of zinc and an outer layer of nickel. It is currently produced with nickel and copper, which costs more than zinc.
Congress passed the Coinage Act in 1792, and the U.S. Mint began producing the penny, known officially as the cent, the following year.
In its nearly 250 years in production, the penny has had multiple facades. It wasn’t until 1909 that it was given its modern-day face, featuring President Abraham Lincoln.
The first penny, produced in 1787, had a sundial design created by Benjamin Franklin. After the U.S. Mint took over, the penny was slightly bigger and included the image of a woman representing Liberty on one side and 15 chain links on the other.
The next penny debuted in 1857, taking on a smaller shape and displaying a flying eagle design on one side and a wreath on the other. It also changed from being 100% copper to 88% copper and 12% nickel. Two years later, an “Indian Head” design was added to one side.
The most recent design from the U.S. Mint was issued in 2010, featuring its “Union Shield” theme. It shows a shield on the tails side of the coin to represent “Lincoln’s preservation of the United States as a single country,” the U.S. Mint wrote.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Brazil ex-President Jair Bolsonaro taken to hospital over abdominal pain
articles.title_zh: Brazil ex-President Jair Bolsonaro taken to hospital over abdominal pain
articles.content_orig:
Convicted former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro , who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest over a coup attempt, has been hospitalized with abdominal pain.
Bolsonaro's son Carlos wrote on X that the former far-right leader was taken to the hospital on Friday and was found to have "a near-complete intestinal obstruction."
The DF Star Hospital in Brasília said that Bolsonaro was suffering from "abdominal distension" and was being examined.
​Bolsonaro, who is 71 years old, ‌has undergone several hospitalizations and surgeries since he was stabbed in the abdomen on the campaign trail for the 2018 elections.
"He is being given medication for pain and an initial attempt to reverse the condition without the need for invasive intervention," Carlos said.
Bolsonaro was in power from 2019 to ​2022. He was convicted last year for plotting a coup after his defeat to current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the 2022 election but claims being the victim of a left-wing judicial witch hunt.
Bolsonaro was placed under humanitarian house arrest on medical grounds.
Carlos on Friday railed against his father's detention, which he blamed for Bolsonaro's current health problems.
Carlos said that the senior Bolsonaro's health was "deteriorating every day in prison due to his lack of mobility" and what he called "the psychological torture he suffers daily."
Another one of Bolsonaro's sons, Flavio Bolsonaro, recently lost the October presidential election to incumbent President Lula . Flavio Bolsonaro left Brazil after the vote and now resides in Florida .

articles.title_orig: Iran Update, November 20, 2026
articles.title_zh: Iran Update, November 20, 2026
articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
Deputy Editor, National Security and Foreign Policy
The rapid advances of a powerful Iran -aligned movement that already rules over most of Yemen 's population threaten the remaining strongholds of Saudi-backed government control and could mark a major victory for the Islamic Republic's regional coalition.
The past week has been a disaster for Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council. The internationally recognized governing body had pledged in September to regain the initiative on the western coast against the rival Ansar Allah, widely known as the Houthis , only to redirect its forces to defend Aden, the de facto seat of government since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014.
Meanwhile, government forces have lost key positions along Yemen's strategically important Red Sea coast, while Taiz, the country's third-largest city, remains surrounded and under siege.
As Saudi Arabia seeks to mobilize a response in support of its ailing ally, Ansar Allah's battlefield momentum marks a major shift for the Iran-led Axis of Resistance that has suffered setbacks elsewhere since the onset of the Middle East crisis more than three years ago.
"In geographic terms, a Houthi victory would be the most important gain for Iran's regional strategy in more than a decade," Arman Mahmoudian, research fellow at the University of South Florida's Global and National Security Institute, told Newsweek . "The government's withdrawal from the Bab el-Mandeb area this weekend already puts the Yemeni side of the strait under Houthi control."
He added: "If Aden falls, the Houthis would hold Yemen's entire Red Sea coast. An actor aligned with Iran would then sit on both of the routes Gulf energy uses to reach world markets: Hormuz, and the Red Sea route Saudi Arabia relies on to get around it. That would partly make up for losing Syria, as the Axis's weight moves from the Levant to the Arabian Peninsula and the Red Sea."
The fall of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's government to insurgents in December 2024 appeared to spell the end of an era for Tehran's regional network of partners.
The development deprived Iran of a key state ally in the Axis of Resistance and disrupted a crucial land route used to supply its regional partners, including Hezbollah in Lebanon. Israel had reached a ceasefire with Hezbollah in November 2024 after a fierce military campaign that killed the movement's longtime secretary-general, Hassan Nasrallah, and other senior commanders and fighters.
But Ansar Allah had demonstrated early on how the sea could be weaponized to even greater effect than land. The group's targeting of commercial vessels severely disrupted traffic through the Red Sea, forcing shipping companies to reroute vessels around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope. The campaign, launched after the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas war in October 2023, demonstrated the Houthis' ability to disrupt one of the world's most important maritime trade routes.
The advances could strengthen Iran's regional network by increasing its ability to threaten shipping through two critical maritime chokepoints: the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
Iran demonstrated its own ability to disrupt global shipping after the U.S.-Israeli war against the Islamic Republic began last February, choking traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. The ongoing conflict brought both Hezbollah and Ansar Allah back into the battle as well, with the latter escalating its operations following a July strike on Sanaa airport by Yemeni government forces operating in coalition with Saudi Arabia.
Having seized the capital in 2014 and subsequently established control over most of Yemen's population, Ansar Allah's advance now resembles a reversal of the situation in Syria as Yemen's government retreats.
At the same time, Mahmoudian pointed out that Ansar Allah's success has granted it greater leverage vis-à-vis its partnership with Iran. Already viewed as "the most independent member of the Axis of Resistance," Ansar Allah has emerged as a formidable actor in its own right, he argued.
"As the rest of the Axis weakened, the Houthis' value grew," Mahmoudian said. "Hamas was devastated, Hezbollah was badly damaged, and Assad's fall cost Iran its land bridge to the Levant. That left the Houthis as the Axis member that is least damaged and most willing to take risks."
"Since the war began in February, the relationship has partly flipped: Iran now needs the Houthis more than they need Iran," he added. "With Iranian ports blockaded and Hormuz contested, the Houthis give Tehran pressure at a second chokepoint, the Bab el-Mandeb."
Barbara Bodine, director of Georgetown University's Institute for the Study of Diplomacy and a former U.S. ambassador to Yemen, defined Ansar Allah's forces as "allies, not proxies, of Iran."
Bodine told Newsweek she was "not the least surprised the Houthis pushed the government forces back," nor was she "the least surprised that the UAE-backed forces (the only credible anti-Houthi forces on the government side) have redeployed to protect Aden, which is the crown jewel of the UAE interest in Yemen."
Questions have long plagued the state of the Yemeni National Army. The remnants of the pre-civil war military have been undermined by years of financial woes, foreign dependence and conflict fatigue, exacerbating existing political, tribal and regional divisions.
Tensions between the forces of the primarily Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council and the largely UAE-sponsored Southern Transitional Council came to a head late last year when the southern separatist faction moved to seize control of parts of southern and eastern Yemen. The initially successful offensive was reversed with Riyadh's aid in January.
This resulted in the apparent dissolution of the Abu Dhabi-backed group, although some members disputed the move. One of the most effective anti-Houthi formations, the Southern Giants Brigades, has continued fighting the latest Ansar Allah advances, though its prospects for lasting success remain uncertain amid ongoing disarray within the broader anti-Ansar Allah front.
"The recent setbacks stem mainly from poor coordination and command and control among anti-Houthi formations, competing political and military agendas, limited resources, and uneven training," Adel Dashela, a researcher at the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies and non-resident fellow at the Finnish Institute in the Middle East, told Newsweek .
"These weaknesses have undermined coordinated operations and common strategic goals," Dashela said. "Differences between Saudi Arabia and the UAE have further complicated coordination and hurt both military and political performance."
Saudi Arabia signaled a recalibration of its approach on Monday, replacing Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad al-Salman with General Fayyad al-Ruwaili as commander of the joint forces. Al-Salman was reassigned as an adviser to the defense minister.
President Donald Trump, whose administration reached a truce with Ansar Allah in May last year, has reportedly rebuffed Saudi requests for direct U.S. military intervention, while Washington continues to focus on its confrontation with Tehran.
Reuters reported Saturday that Trump was considering holding off on further strikes against Iran unless Tehran or Ansar Allah carried out new provocations, citing three people familiar with the matter.
But while an Ansar Allah victory would constitute a setback for the competing visions of both Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, the reverberations would be felt far beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Dashela argued that consolidating control over the mountainous highlands of Taiz and Lahj "would give the group a strategic advantage" in its bid to wield influence over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, "a vital artery of global trade."
